front: Kernel level thread support: what must the kernel maintain?
back: A data structure to represent threads, plus the scheduling and syncing mechanisms to make multithreading correct and efficient.

front: User level thread support: what does the library provide?
back: A user level library linked with the application provides all management and support for threads: the data structure and the scheduling mechanisms.

front: What does a user level thread data structure contain (single CPU)?
back:
• thread ids
  • thread registers
  • thread stacks
source: Thread Related Data Structures: Single CPU

front: Why split the process control block into smaller structures for multiple kernel level threads?
back: So we don't have to replicate the entire PCB in each KLT. The stack and registers are broken out (different per KLT) and stored in the KLT data structure; the PCB keeps the virtual address mappings and everything relevant to the whole process.
source: Thread Related Data Structures: Single CPU

front: From the user level threading library's perspective, what do the underlying kernel level threads look like?
back: Virtual CPUs. The library decides which of its user level threads to schedule onto them.
source: Thread Related Data Structures: Single CPU

front: On Unix-based systems, which operations are useful for saving and restoring the context of a user level thread?
back: setjmp and longjmp.
source: Thread Related Data Structures: Single CPU

front: Thread data structures at scale: what relationships must be maintained between ULTs, PCB, and KLTs?
back:
• ULT library tracks all ULTs of a process, so ULTs relate to the PCB
  • Per process: track the KLTs executing on its behalf
  • Per KLT: track the process on whose behalf it executes

front: At scale with multiple CPUs, what additional data structure and relationship are needed?
back: A data structure to represent the CPUs, plus a relationship between the kernel level threads and the CPUs they execute on. For example, a KLT records the CPU it has affinity to or last ran on, and a CPU points to its current thread and to the threads that typically run there.

front: When the kernel is multithreaded, how does it decide whether to swap the entire PCB on a context switch between KLTs?
back: Each KLT points to the PCB of the process it executes for. Switching between KLTs of different processes, the kernel quickly sees they point to different PCBs, hence different virtual address mappings, so it invalidates the existing mappings and restores the new ones, saving the entire PCB of the first KLT and restoring that of the second.

front: Define hard process state.
back: The portion of the PCB that is relevant for all user level threads in a given process (e.g. virtual address mapping).

front: Define light process state.
back: The portion of the PCB relevant only for a subset of user level threads associated with a particular kernel level thread (e.g. signals, system call arguments).

front: Rationale for data structures: list the four drawbacks of a single large control block.
back:
• large continuous data structure
  • private for each entity
  • saved and restored in entirety on each context switch
  • updates may be challenging

front: Rationale for data structures: list the four advantages of multiple data structures.
back:
• smaller data structures
  • easier to share
  • save and restore only what needs to change on context switch
  • user-level library only needs to update a portion of the state for customized behavior

text: The single control block is worse on four counts: {{c1::scalability}} (size), {{c2::overhead}} (private copies), {{c3::performance}} (full save/restore), and {{c4::flexibility}} (updates touch multiple OS services).

front: Thread structures quiz: in Linux 3.17, what is the name of the kernel thread structure, and where is it declared?
back: kthread_worker, declared in kthread.h. Together with the functions in that header it provides a simple interface for creating and stopping kernel threads.

front: Thread structures quiz: which member of Linux 3.17's kthread_worker describes the process the kernel thread is running?
back: The task_struct, which holds most of the important information about a process. Of the four members, the spinlock and the list_head do not describe a process.

front: User level structures in Solaris 2.0: which paper describes the threading model and user level thread data structures?
back: Stein & Shah, Implementing Lightweight Threads.

front: User level structures in Solaris 2.0: which paper describes the kernel level structures?
back: Eykholt et al., Beyond Multiprocessing: Multithreading the SunOS Kernel.

front: Solaris 2.0: is the lightweight threads library described by Stein & Shah pthreads?
back: No. It is not pthreads, but it is a similar kind of user level threading library.

front: Solaris 2.0 threading model: what mappings and CPU/kernel assumptions apply?
back: Multiple-CPU platform with a multithreaded kernel; processes may be single or multithreaded; both many:many and one:one ULT:KLT mappings are supported.

front: Solaris 2.0: what data structure is associated with each KLT executing on behalf of a ULT, and what does it represent to the library?
back: A lightweight process (LWP). From the user level library's perspective, LWPs are the virtual CPUs onto which ULTs are scheduled.

front: Solaris 2.0: when the library creates a thread, what does the returned thread id actually point to?
back: It is not a direct pointer to the thread data structure; it is an index into an array of thread pointers. If the thread has a problem, a raw pointer would just point to corrupt memory; with a table index, the library can encode information in the table entry that gives meaningful feedback or an error message.

front: Solaris 2.0: what fields does the user level thread data structure contain?
back:
• execution context
  • registers
  • signal mask
  • priority
  • stack pointer
  • thread local storage
  • stack

front: Solaris 2.0 ULT structure: what does thread local storage hold?
back: The variables defined in the thread functions that are known at compile time, so the compiler can allocate private storage for each of them on a per-thread basis.

front: Solaris 2.0 ULT structure: where can a thread's stack size come from?
back: From the library defaults, or the user can provide a stack.

front: Solaris 2.0: why can threads be stored contiguously, and how does the scheduler find the next one?
back: The size of a thread data structure is almost entirely known at compile time, allowing compact contiguous layout (locality). The scheduler finds a thread by multiplying the thread index by the size of the data structure.

front: Compact contiguous thread layout: what problem can stack overrun cause, and when is it detected?
back: The user library does not control stack growth, and the OS does not know there are multiple ULTs. One thread can overrun its boundary and overwrite the next thread's data. The error is not detected until the overwritten thread runs, even though the overwriting thread caused it.

front: Define a red zone (lecture framing).
back: A portion of the virtual address space that is not allocated, placed to separate thread information. Writing to it causes the OS to fault, associating the error with the problematic thread.

front: Lecture says threads are packed contiguously and found by index. How does Stein & Shah describe where the thread structure lives?
back: The thread structure does not contain TLS; it is allocated in thread-local storage (TLS), along with a private copy of errno, rather than as a separate fixed-size record. The library carves TLS from the base of each new thread's stack, with size _etls computed by the run-time linker at program start; on SPARC register %g7 points to the current thread's TLS.

front: Lecture describes the red zone as an unallocated gap between threads. What exactly is it per Stein & Shah?
back: The invalid page the library places after each stack it allocates (library stacks are mapped-in anonymous memory), so the process is signalled if a thread runs off its stack. An application supplying its own stacks can add a red zone or pack stacks its own way.

front: Kernel level structures in Solaris 2.0: what does the kernel maintain for each process?
back:
• list of kernel level threads
  • virtual address space
  • user credentials
  • signal handlers

front: What data does the lightweight process (LWP) contain, and who can see it?
back:
• user level registers
  • system call arguments
  • resource usage info
  • signal masks
Similar to the ULT data but visible to the kernel for scheduling decisions.

front: How does the kernel find aggregate resource usage for an entire process?
back: Resource usage is tracked per KLT in each LWP, so the kernel must walk through all of the LWPs associated with the process.

front: What does the kernel level thread structure contain?
back:
• kernel-level registers
  • stack pointer
  • scheduling info
  • pointers to the associated LWP, process, and CPU structures

front: Why is the kernel level thread data not swappable, while the LWP data is?
back: OS services (e.g. scheduler) need KLT info even when the thread is inactive, so it must stay resident. The LWP data is not needed when the process is not running, so under memory pressure it can be swapped out, supporting more threads in less memory.

front: What does the CPU data structure contain?
back:
• current thread
  • list of kernel level threads
  • dispatching & interrupt handling information

front: On SPARC machines, what makes identifying the currently executing thread easier?
back: A dedicated register holds the thread that is currently executing.

front: Lecture lists the CPU structure as holding a list of kernel level threads. What does Eykholt et al. actually say the cpu structure points to and how are threads linked?
back: The cpu structure points to the currently executing thread and to that CPU's idle thread, and holds current dispatching and interrupt handling info. Thread structures are linked on a per-process list and a system-wide list of all threads; the paper describes no per-CPU list of kernel threads.

front: Solaris 2.0 kernel structures: what does the process data structure point to, and what does each kernel level thread structure point to?
back: The process holds information about the user, points to the virtual address mapping data structure, and points to a list of kernel level threads. Each KLT structure points to its LWP and its stack, which is swappable.

front: Basic thread management: why might an application request a fixed, limited number of kernel threads?
back: The OS may cap the number of KLTs it supports. Given its actual concurrency (e.g. two threads running while two block on IO), the application requests only as many KLTs as it needs (e.g. two).

front: Basic thread management: in the Linux 3.17 source, what minimum number of threads does fork.c guarantee at boot, and which variable holds the thread limit?
back: At least 20 threads, so the OS can boot. The limit is held in max_threads.

front: Basic thread management: what system call lets an application request a specific number of kernel level threads, and in pthreads?
back: set_concurrency; in pthreads, pthread_setconcurrency.

front: PThread concurrency quiz: what does passing 0 to pthread_setconcurrency mean, and where does the call have any effect?
back: 0 asks the implementation to decide. (Beyond the lecture: the call is only a hint and is meaningful only on many:many implementations; on Linux (1:1) it has no effect.)

front: Basic thread management: what happens if the two user threads scheduled on the KLTs are the two that block?
back: The KLTs block too, so the whole process is blocked even though other ULTs could make progress. The library has no way to know the KLTs are about to block, so it cannot react beforehand.

front: Basic thread management: what kernel/library interaction does the lecture propose so the process does not block when both KLTs block?
back:
1. The kernel signals the library before blocking
  2. The library checks its run queue, sees runnable ULTs, and makes a system call requesting more KLTs (LWPs)
  3. The kernel allocates one and the library schedules the remaining ULTs onto it
  4. Later, once the I/O completes, the kernel notices one KLT is almost always idle and tells the library it no longer has access to it

front: Basic thread management: why do the user level library and kernel need system calls and special signals to coordinate?
back: They have no insight into one another; the kernel exposes system calls and special signals so the kernel and the ULT library can interact and coordinate.

front: Lecture calls the concurrency hint a system call named set_concurrency. How does Stein & Shah describe the interface and what the library does with it?
back: It is thr_setconcurrency(), a threads library call, not a system call. The library ensures at least n LWPs in its pool (or one per thread if fewer than n threads) and creates them itself; growth beyond n comes from SIGWAITING.

front: Lecture suggests the kernel signals the library before blocking. What does Stein & Shah say Solaris actually does?
back: Solaris does not notify before blocking. The kernel sends SIGWAITING when it detects all LWPs in the process are blocked in indefinite waits; if there are runnable threads the library creates a new LWP. Per-block notification is what scheduler activations (Anderson et al.) provide.

front: Thread management visibility: what does the kernel see vs. what does the user level library see?
back: Kernel sees: KLTs, CPUs, kernel level scheduler. Library sees: ULTs, available KLTs. In 1:1 the library sees as many KLTs as ULTs, but the kernel manages them.

front: Thread management visibility: how does the lecture relate binding a ULT to thread pinning, and which ULTs are bound in a 1:1 model?
back: Binding a ULT to a KLT is analogous to permanently associating a KLT with a CPU on a multi-CPU system, which is called thread pinning; "bound" is the term Solaris threads introduced for the ULT-to-KLT case. In a 1:1 model every ULT is bound.

front: Thread management: what goes wrong if a ULT holding a lock is preempted (via its KLT) in a many:many model?
back: The library scheduler cycles through remaining ULTs; any needing the lock cannot run, so time is wasted until the lock-holding thread is rescheduled.

front: Thread management visibility: in the many:many model, what does the kernel not know about that pushes the lecture toward 1:1?
back: The user level library makes scheduling changes that alter the ULT:KLT mapping without the kernel knowing, and the kernel is unaware of user level data structures such as mutexes and wait queues.

front: When does the process jump to the user level library scheduler?
back:
• ULTs explicitly yield
  • a timer set by the UL library expires
  • ULTs call library functions like lock/unlock
  • blocked threads become runnable
Also in response to certain signals from timers and/or the kernel.

front: Lecture introduces binding by analogy to thread pinning. What reason does Stein & Shah give for binding?
back: Global scheduling scope, for a thread needing real-time response such as mouse tracking. A bound thread calling priocntl() changes the LWP it is bound to so it can run in the real-time class ahead of unbound threads; the paper does not mention pinning.

front: Lecture lists a UL-library timer expiry as a trigger for the scheduler. What does Stein & Shah say about user-level time slicing and preemption?
back: The paper describes no user-level time slicing; threads compete for LWPs by priority. An active thread is preempted only when a newly runnable thread has higher priority (or the active thread's priority is lowered below a runnable thread's). The library does it by setting a flag in the thread structure and sending the thread's LWP a SIGLWP.

front: Issue on multiple CPUs: describe the T1/T2/T3 priority scenario and the core problem.
back: T3 highest, T2 mid, T1 lowest. T2 holds the mutex on one CPU, T3 blocks for it, T1 runs on the other CPU. When T2 releases the mutex, T3 becomes runnable, so T1 (lowest) must be preempted. The realization is made in the library as T2 unlocks; we must preempt a thread on a different CPU.

front: Issue on multiple CPUs: how does one CPU cause the required scheduling change on another CPU?
back: It cannot directly modify another CPU's registers. It sends a signal to the thread's context on the other CPU, telling that CPU to run the library code locally so the proper scheduling decision (block T1, schedule T3) is made.

front: Synchronization: on a multiprocessor, why might blocking T4 on the mutex queue be wasteful?
back: By the time T4 is placed on the queue, T1 may already have released the mutex. If the critical section is very short, spinning is more efficient than paying the cost of blocking and later retrieval. If the critical section is long, blocking makes more sense, since spinning burns CPU cycles.

front: Define an adaptive mutex and when it makes sense (lecture).
back: A mutex that sometimes blocks and sometimes spins. It only makes sense on multiprocessor systems, since spinning is only worthwhile if the mutex owner is currently executing in parallel.

front: Synchronization: what information must be stored to decide whether to spin or block (lecture)?
back: Information about the mutex owner (whether it is currently running on a CPU, which favors spinning) and the length of the critical section.

front: Define death row and the reaper (lecture).
back: When a thread exits its data structures are not freed immediately; it is marked as on death row. A special reaper thread periodically garbage-collects them. A new thread request arriving first can reuse a death-row structure, giving performance gains.

front: Lecture says the adaptive mutex uses critical-section length to decide spin vs. block. How does Eykholt et al. describe MUTEX_DEFAULT?
back: It spins while the recorded owner is running on a processor, checked by polling whether any CPU's current-thread pointer equals the owner, and sleeps once the owner stops running; on a uniprocessor it always sleeps. Critical-section length is not an input.

front: Death row: lecture says exiting threads go on death row. Which threads does Stein & Shah say go there, and what happens to the others?
back: Only detached threads go on death row. An undetached thread goes on a zombie list and is reaped by the thread that calls thr_join() on it.

front: Stein & Shah: when does the reaper run, and why does the reaping rate affect thread creation speed?
back: It runs when there are idle LWPs or when death row is full. It frees the stacks of threads that used library-allocated stacks, and the freed stacks are kept for reuse, which is why the reaping rate affects the speed of thread creation.

front: Define interrupts and name components that deliver them.
back: Events generated externally by components other than the CPU to which they are delivered; notifications that an external event occurred. Sources: I/O devices, timers, other CPUs.

front: Do interrupts appear synchronously or asynchronously?
back: Asynchronously; they do not appear in response to any specific action on the CPU.

front: Define signals and what determines which can occur.
back: Events triggered by the CPU and the software running on it. Which signals can occur depends on the operating system; two identical platforms running different OSes have the same interrupts but different signals.

front: Can signals appear synchronously, asynchronously, or both?
back: Both. Synchronously in direct response to a CPU action (e.g. touching unallocated memory), or asynchronously like interrupts.

front: Signal/interrupt similarities: how are interrupts and signals identified?
back: Each has a unique identifier, whose values depend on the hardware (interrupts) or the operating system (signals).

front: Signal/interrupt similarities: at what granularity is each masked, and why?
back: An interrupt is masked per CPU (interrupts are delivered to the CPU as a whole); a signal is masked per process (signals are delivered to individual processes).

front: What does a mask do, and who specifies interrupt vs. signal handlers?
back: A mask disables or delays notification of an incoming interrupt or signal. Interrupt handlers are specified for the entire system by the OS; signal handlers are set per-process by the process itself.

front: Lecture masks signals per process. What granularity does Stein & Shah give for signal masks, and what is shared?
back: Each thread has its own signal mask and each LWP has its own mask; only the set of signal handlers is shared by the whole process. Linux signal(7) agrees: masks are per thread, handlers per process.

front: Visual metaphor (toy shop): what corresponds to an interrupt and what to a signal, and why?
back:
• Interrupt: a snowstorm warning, caused by an event external to the shop, as an interrupt is generated by an event external to the CPU
  • Signal: a battery-is-low warning, caused from within by the worker fixing a toy, as a signal is generated by the software running on the CPU

front: Visual metaphor: what three qualities do toy shop warnings share with interrupts and signals?
back:
• Handled in specific ways: safety protocols or hazard plans; for interrupts and signals, the handler
  • Can be ignored: the worker may just continue; interrupts and signals can be masked
  • Can be expected or unexpected: dead batteries happen regularly, a snowstorm depends on where the shop is; interrupts and signals can appear synchronously or asynchronously

front: Interrupt handling: how is an incoming interrupt uniquely identified, and what message type do modern devices use?
back: By the pins where the interrupt is received or by the message itself. In the past interrupts used dedicated wires; most modern devices use a message signaled interrupt (MSI), carried on the same interconnect that connects the device to the CPU complex (e.g. PCI Express).

front: Interrupt handling: how does the CPU find and run the handler, and in whose context?
back: If the interrupt is enabled, the CPU looks up the interrupt number in the interrupt handler table, which maps it to the handler's starting address, sets the program counter there, and runs it. This happens in the context of the interrupted thread.

text: Which interrupts can occur depends on the {{c1::hardware}} of the platform; how they are handled depends on the {{c2::operating system}}.

front: Signal handling: give an example of an OS-generated signal and its number.
back: Accessing unallocated memory makes the OS generate SIGSEGV, signal 11 in Linux.

front: Signal handling: how does the OS route a generated signal to its handler?
back: Per process, the OS maintains a mapping from signal number to the starting address of a handling routine. When a signal is generated, the program counter is adjusted to point to that process's handler for that signal.

front: List the OS default signal responses.
back:
• Terminate
  • Ignore
  • Terminate and Core Dump
  • Stop
  • Continue (from stopped)

front: Signal handling: what is the default action for SIGSEGV, and why?
back: Terminate and core dump, so the core dump can be inspected to determine why the process crashed.

front: Signal handling: how does a process install a custom handler, and is every signal catchable?
back: Through a system call like signal or sigaction. Not all signals can be caught.

front: Give examples of synchronous vs. asynchronous signals.
back: Synchronous: SIGSEGV, SIGFPE (divide by zero), SIGKILL (sent from one process to another). Asynchronous: SIGKILL (as the receiver), SIGALARM (timer expiration).

front: Signals quiz: name the POSIX signal for each event: terminal interrupt; "high bandwidth" data on a socket; background process attempting to write; file size limit exceeded.
back:
• Terminal interrupt: SIGINT
  • Socket data: SIGURG, actually raised for out-of-band (urgent) data, nothing to do with bandwidth
  • Background write: SIGTTOU, only for a background process group writing to its controlling terminal with TOSTOP set
  • File size limit exceeded: SIGXFSZ

front: Why can handling signals/interrupts on the interrupted thread's stack cause a deadlock?
back: The handler runs on the thread's stack with the same stack pointer. If the handler needs a mutex the interrupted thread already locked, the thread can't unlock until the handler returns, but the handler can't return until it locks the mutex: deadlock.

front: Why disable interrupts or signals: what happens on the thread's stack when multiple interrupts or signals arrive?
back: The stack pointer stays the same, so whatever the thread was doing is still on its stack, and multiple interrupts or signals keep stacking their handlers on the stack of the thread that was originally interrupted.

front: Handler/mutex deadlock: besides masks, what simpler fix exists, and why is it rejected?
back: Enforce that handler code stays simple and never does things like acquire mutexes. It is too restrictive.

front: What is a signal/interrupt mask and how is it structured?
back: A mechanism to dynamically decide whether signals/interrupts can interrupt a thread. It is a sequence of bits, one per interrupt/signal, where the value (0 or 1) signifies disabled or enabled.

front: What happens when an event occurs and its mask bit is enabled vs. disabled?
back: Enabled: proceed with the handling code. Disabled: the interrupt/signal is made pending and handled later when the mask changes.

front: How do masks solve the handler/mutex deadlock?
back: Disable the interrupt/signal before acquiring the mutex and re-enable it after releasing the mutex, so we are never in handler code while the mutex is locked. The pending interrupt/signal runs once re-enabled.

front: If a signal is generated multiple times while pending, will the handler run that many times?
back: No. The handling routine typically runs only once, so generating the signal more than once is not sufficient to guarantee multiple executions.

front: More on masks: what granularity are interrupt masks vs. signal masks, and what is the effect of disabling?
back: Interrupt masks are per CPU: a disabled interrupt is not delivered to the CPU by the routing mechanism. Signal masks are per execution context (ULT on top of KLT): a disabled signal is not delivered to that context by the kernel.

front: Interrupts on multicore: what strategy improves performance, and how?
back: The routing logic sends an interrupt to any CPU with it enabled. Enabling interrupts on just one CPU avoids interrupt-handling overhead and perturbation on the other cores, improving performance.

front: Define one-shot signals.
back: Signals handled at least once; to the ULT, n signals may look like one. The handling routine must be explicitly re-enabled each time. If a custom handler is not reinstalled, the next instance uses the OS default (and is lost if the default is to ignore).

front: Define real-time signals.
back: Signals that interrupt as many times as they are raised; n signals call the handler n times. They queue rather than override. Linux, for example, supports real-time signals.

front: Interrupts as threads: how does handling an interrupt in its own thread avoid the mutex deadlock?
back: When the handler thread tries to acquire the mutex it blocks like any other thread (placed on the mutex wait queue) instead of deadlocking. The original thread is rescheduled, eventually unlocks the mutex, and the handler thread is dequeued to complete.

front: Interrupts as threads (lecture framing): since dynamic thread creation is expensive, how does the lecture say Solaris decides whether to make a handler a thread?
back: The rule (as the lecture describes the SunOS paper): if the handler routine contains no locks it cannot block, so it runs on the interrupted thread's stack. Only if the handler might lock a mutex is it turned into a real thread.

front: Interrupts as threads: how is the cost of dynamic thread creation eliminated?
back: The kernel pre-creates and pre-initializes thread structures for supported interrupt routines, pointing them at the handler and allocating internal data upfront, so the creation cost is not paid when an interrupt occurs. Thread creation is thereby removed from the fast path of interrupt processing, which significantly speeds up interrupt handling.

front: Lecture says SunOS handles interrupts in their own threads. Which interrupts does Eykholt et al. say are not handled as threads?
back: Interrupts above a tunable thread level are not handled as threads and can synchronize only through spin mutexes and software interrupts. Thread level is normally the maximum priority; it is lowered, typically to the interrupt level of the scheduling clock, only where firmware cannot tolerate the short dispatcher lockout.

front: Lecture frames the choice as creating a thread only if the handler locks. What does Eykholt et al. say SunOS 5.0 actually does on an interrupt?
back: It does the minimum work to move onto the stack of a preallocated interrupt thread and makes it the current thread; the interrupted thread is pinned until the interrupt thread returns or blocks. Only if the interrupt thread blocks does it save state and become a full thread. Handling interrupts on the interrupted process's kernel stack, or on a separate interrupt stack, is the traditional UNIX scheme the paper replaces.

front: Interrupts: once handling is passed to a separate thread, what can happen to interrupts disabled when the interrupt first occurred, and why is it safe?
back: They can be re-enabled. Interrupts arriving now are handled as for any other thread in the system, so there is no additional danger of deadlock.

front: Interrupt handling top vs. bottom half: define the top half.
back: Runs in the context of the interrupted thread, before the handler thread is created. Executes immediately, so it must be fast, non-blocking, and do minimal processing.

front: Interrupt handling top vs. bottom half: define the bottom half.
back: Everything that runs once the handler thread is created. It can have arbitrary complexity: like any other thread it can be scheduled later and can block. Other than timeouts associated with the device, nothing restricts when it runs.

front: Interrupts top vs. bottom half: what is the takeaway for permitting arbitrary functionality in interrupt handling?
back: The handling routine must be executed by another thread that we can synchronize with and that is allowed to block.

front: Which OS uses the names top half and bottom half for the two parts of interrupt processing?
back: Linux.

front: Lecture presents a top half / bottom half split. What two-level design does Eykholt et al. reject, and why?
back: The two-level design where a bounded first-level handler wakes a second-level thread; rejected because it requires restructured drivers and always costs a full context switch. SunOS 5.0 runs the whole handler on the interrupt thread and pays for a full thread only on lock contention. Oracle's driver guide uses a split of this kind only for high-level interrupts, through soft interrupts.

front: Performance of threads as interrupts: what is the added per-interrupt overhead, and what is saved per mutex operation?
back: About 40 SPARC instructions added per interrupt handling operation. It is no longer necessary to change the interrupt mask around locking a mutex, saving about 12 instructions per mutex operation.

front: Performance of threads as interrupts: why is the net instruction count decreased?
back: Mutex lock/unlocks occur much more frequently than interrupts, so the 12 instructions saved per mutex op outweigh the ~40 added per interrupt. It optimizes for the common case.

front: Performance of threads as interrupts: how does this design apply 'optimize for the common case', and what constraint must the optimization respect?
back: The common case is mutex lock/unlock, so it is made as efficient as possible and the cost is paid elsewhere. Safety and correctness cannot be sacrificed, so another technique must compensate, here handling interrupts as threads; this is good practice as long as the net effect is positive.

front: Lecture says ~40 SPARC instructions are added and implies a thread is created per interrupt. What does Eykholt et al. clarify?
back: The added overhead is about 40 SPARC instructions, but no thread is created per interrupt: interrupt threads are preallocated, and converting one into a full thread is done only when there is lock contention.

front: Threads and signal handling: where do the ULT and KLT signal masks live, and who sees each?
back: Each ULT has its own mask living at user level, visible to the library but not the kernel. Each KLT also has a mask, living in the LWP attached to that KLT, visible only to the kernel.

front: Threads and signal handling: when a ULT disables a signal, why does the kernel still think it is enabled?
back: The ULT clears the bit in its own mask entirely at user level, so the kernel level mask is not updated; from the kernel's point of view the signal is still enabled.

front: Threads and signal handling: what is the library wrapper and why install it?
back: The library (not the application) installs a wrapper around each signal's real handler, so the library always sees the signal first. The library can see every ULT's mask, letting it update masks at user level and avoid a system call on each mask change.

front: Threads and signal handling, Case 1: kernel mask and the running ULT's mask both enabled. What happens?
back: The kernel delivers the signal to the currently running ULT, that thread handles it, and there is no problem.

front: Threads and signal handling, Case 2: kernel enabled, running ULT disabled, but a runnable (not running) ULT is enabled. What does the library do?
back: The wrapper sees all ULT masks; it invokes the library scheduler to swap in the ULT that can handle the signal, then passes the signal to that thread's handler.

front: Threads and signal handling, Case 3: the enabled ULT is already running on another KLT/CPU. How is the signal delivered?
back: The wrapper on the KLT whose ULT is disabled sends a directed signal to the LWP (KLT) where the enabled ULT runs. The kernel delivers it there, the wrapper kicks in, sees the running ULT can handle it, and lets the real handler run.

front: Threads and signal handling, Case 4: every ULT has the signal disabled but kernel masks are still 1. What does the library do?
back: The wrapper makes a system call to disable the signal in the current KLT's mask. It cannot change the masks of KLTs on other CPUs, so it reissues the signal to the entire process; the kernel delivers it to another KLT whose mask is still enabled, and the wrapper repeats. This continues until every kernel mask in the process has the signal disabled.

front: Case 4: lecture says the library reissues the signal to the entire process. What does Stein & Shah say the global handler does?
back: It resends the signal to the process if it was undirected, or to the same LWP if it was directed; the kernel's signal delivery information lets it tell the two apart.

front: Threads and signal handling: after Case 4, what must happen when a ULT re-enables the signal?
back: The library makes a system call to re-enable the signal in one kernel level mask, so the kernel again sees the process as capable of handling it.

front: Threads and signal handling: what is the common-case optimization in this scheme?
back: Mask updates are frequent, cheap, and done at user level without system calls; signals are rare, so making signal handling more expensive (possible system calls to fix discrepancies) is an acceptable tradeoff.

front: Tasks in Linux: what is a task and how does it map to processes?
back: A task is the execution context of a kernel level thread. A single-threaded process has one task; a multithreaded process has many tasks.

front: Tasks in Linux: how is a task identified, and how is a multithreaded process identified?
back: Each task has a task identifier which, for historic reasons and somewhat misleadingly, is called pid_t pid. In a multithreaded process each task has a different pid; the process is identified by the pid of the first task created, captured in pid_t tgid (task group id).

front: Tasks in Linux: what does struct list_head tasks provide?
back: The head of the list of all of the tasks for a process. Walking this list is another way to find the process id of a group of tasks.

front: Tasks in Linux: how did Linux always represent process state, and how do tasks share state?
back: Never one contiguous PCB; always a collection of data structures pointing to each other (e.g. struct mm_struct *mm, struct files_struct *files). Tasks share state by pointing at the same structure.

front: Tasks in Linux: roughly how large is the task structure?
back: Roughly 1.7 KB, so it holds much more than the key elements shown in the lecture.

front: Tasks in Linux: what does clone take, and what does sharing_flags control?
back: It takes a function pointer and an argument (like pthread_create) plus sharing_flags, which denotes which portion of the task state is shared between parent and child.

front: Tasks in Linux: what do all sharing flags set vs. all cleared produce, and how is fork implemented?
back: All set: a new thread sharing state with the parent. All cleared: shares nothing, akin to a new process. fork is implemented by clone with all sharing flags cleared.

front: Tasks in Linux: how do fork semantics differ for single- vs. multithreaded processes?
back: Forking a single-threaded process gives a full replica of the parent. Forking a multithreaded process gives a single-threaded child, replicating only the state visible from the task that called fork.

front: Tasks in Linux: what is NPTL, what model does it use, and what did it replace?
back: The Native POSIX Threads Library (NPTL), a 1:1 model (one kernel task per ULT). It replaced LinuxThreads, which was very similar to the many-to-many model described in the Solaris papers and suffered from the same complexity in signal management.

front: Tasks in Linux: in NPTL, what does the kernel see about each user level thread?
back: The kernel sees every ULT, including whether it is blocked on synchronization and what its signal mask is.

front: Tasks in Linux: why is NPTL's 1:1 model acceptable despite the kernel seeing every ULT?
back: Kernel trapping has become much cheaper, so user/kernel crossings (e.g. updating the kernel level signal mask) are affordable; modern platforms have more memory, removing the constraint to keep KLT counts small; and the range of thread IDs is not a practical restriction for common processes. Together these remove the main reasons for the many-to-many model.

front: Tasks in Linux: when might it make sense to revisit user level thread support beyond the 1:1 model?
back: For extremely large numbers of threads (e.g. exascale computing) or complex heterogeneous platforms with different kinds of processors. For most practical purposes the 1:1 model is sufficient.
